rows.description: A mature person notices the racing heart or urge to run, snap or please, pauses, breathes slowly and chooses a response. The aim is not to erase the alarm but to avoid being run by it.

rows.description: A young child says their tummy hurts on school mornings because worry lives in the body and the child has no words for it. The pain is real, and gentle talk about fears usually helps more than argument about whether it is true.

related mind states: fear, anxiety, hurt

rows.subtype: Child who cannot say what is wrong [Actor]
rows.description: An anxious child may complain of headaches, tight chest or shaky legs before tests, and refuse activities. Teaching simple words such as worried and nervous connects the body signals to feelings.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: anxiety

rows.subtype: Parent unsure whether to push or protect [Receiver]
rows.description: A parent of an anxious child may swing between forcing bravery and removing every difficulty. Small steady steps with warm encouragement, not avoidance and not pressure, help a child build tolerance.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Racing thoughts and tension before exams [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager feels tight shoulders, shallow breath, restless legs and looping what-if thoughts about results and family expectations. Preparation, breaks and slow breathing ease the body, while catastrophic thinking feeds it.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: boredom, relief from stress

rows.subtype: Anxiety mistaken for laziness or attitude [Observer]
rows.description: A teacher or friend may read avoidance, missed deadlines and irritability as carelessness when a student is actually anxious. Asking kindly what is hard lets the student explain and find support.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A young adult lives with tightness in the chest, poor sleep, jaw clenching and a mind that scans for problems. Regular movement, honest talk and, when it persists, help from a qualified professional can ease it.

rows.subtype: Self-soothing that helps rather than hides [Response]
rows.description: A person learns grounding steps such as feeling feet on the floor, slowing the exhale and naming what they see, and does not rely on avoidance or numbing habits. If worry keeps ruling life, they seek professional help.

rows.description: A child or preteen may suddenly feel a pounding heart, dizziness and fear of dying or going mad, with no obvious trigger. It feels terrifying, though the sensations pass, and calm adult presence matters most.

rows.subtype: Teen scared of the fear itself [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager after a panic episode may dread another and start avoiding classrooms, buses or crowds. The fear of the sensations keeps the cycle going, and understanding what panic is loosens its grip.
